passage:
For a year Lalremsiami had spent nights raging online about the road to her village near Champhai. The contractors had taken the money, the monsoon had taken the road, and the posts she read blamed whole groups of people for it. She had begun to hate faces she'd never met.
In spring she stopped. She handed her phone to her mother every night at nine. She slept. She talked twice with the counsellor at the district hospital.
The anger stayed, but she aimed it. With Tushar, the young schoolteacher, she walked the road with a notebook and photographed every broken stretch. They collected forty-one signatures and took the file to the village council, then to the block office, politely, twice.
In October a survey team came. Nothing was fixed yet. But when Tushar asked if she was still angry, she said, "Yes. At the road. Not at people."

qa.q: How many signatures did they collect?
qa.a: Forty-one signatures.

qa.q: What does Lalremsiami mean by 'At the road. Not at people'?
qa.a: She still feels angry about the injustice, but calmer, having let go of hatred for people she had never met.

qa.q: Which steps helped her redirect the anger?
qa.a: Giving up the phone at night, sleeping, seeing a counsellor, and lawful action: documenting the road and taking signatures to the council and block office.

qa.q: How might Tushar see Lalremsiami's change?
qa.a: Tushar likely sees a determined, steady partner and feels encouraged working beside her.

grounding: A young woman in a village steps back from rage feeds, sleeps, sees a counsellor and turns her grievance into lawful local action.

Hi Sonali didi,
You'll be proud of me. Yesterday I got a message that said it was from the bank: "Your account will be blocked today. Share the OTP and pay a fee through gift cards to unblock. Keep this confidential." It had the bank's logo and everything. My heart was going fast, because it's the account Papa opened for my scholarship.
Then I remembered what you said at Diwali: real banks never ask for OTPs, secrecy or gift cards, and never rush you. Pause first.
So I didn't reply. I showed Papa. We turned the bank card over and called the number printed on the back, not the one in the message. The bank person said, "This is a scam, please don't share anything." Papa reported the message the same evening.
Papa said I handled it better than he would have. I'm still a bit shaky, honestly. But mostly happy.
Naveen

qa.a: The number printed on the back of the bank card.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel when the message first arrived?
qa.a: Naveen felt scared and rushed, heart going fast because it was the scholarship account.

qa.q: What rule helped Naveen, and why does it work?
qa.a: Pause and check through the official number; scams depend on urgency and secrecy, which a pause and a real call break.

qa.q: How might Sonali didi feel reading this email?
qa.a: Sonali would likely feel proud and relieved that the Diwali advice worked when it mattered.

grounding: A teen recognises that a real bank never demands secrecy, instant payment or gift cards, pauses, and checks through the official number.

Sudha, okay, so you know I've been playing that football game for months. Last week I got a message: "Congratulations, you've won a rare player pack! Buy two gift cards within ten minutes to claim, and don't tell anyone or it gets cancelled." A timer was ticking on the screen. My hands were literally sweating. I'd wanted that pack forever.
But three things felt off. Real companies don't want gift cards. They don't give you ten minutes. And why would a prize need to be secret?
So I closed it. Didn't click anything. I told my mum, and we found the game company's official support page ourselves, not through the link. They said they never send messages like that. Mum and I reported it together.
The silly part? I still wanted the pack. But I'd rather lose a fake prize than real money. Akash's rule: if it's urgent and secret, it's fake.

qa.a: Within ten minutes.

qa.a: Akash felt tempted and anxious, hands sweating, because it was a prize wanted for a long time.

qa.a: Pausing, spotting the gift cards, rush and secrecy, telling Mum, and checking the official support page directly.

I was doing homework at the dining table when Simran's phone rang, and she put it on speaker by mistake. A man said he was from the cyber police and that a parcel in her name contained illegal items. "You must pay a fine now or we come to your house. Do not tell your parents. This is confidential."
Simran's face went white. I thought she'd burst into tears. But she took a slow breath and said, "I'm fourteen. I'll call you back after checking." The man began shouting. She hung up.
Then she walked straight to the kitchen and told our mother. Jahnavi didn't panic. She found the official cyber-crime helpline number on the government website, called it, and reported the caller's number while Simran sat beside her.
I don't know exactly what Simran was feeling. Her hands were shaking. But she did everything right.

qa.q: Who did the caller claim to be?
qa.a: From the cyber police.

qa.q: What might Simran have felt when the caller demanded secrecy?
qa.a: She was likely terrified, face white and hands shaking, yet calm enough to pause.

qa.q: Which of Simran's actions protected her, and why?
qa.a: Hanging up and telling her mother at once; real police do not demand secret, instant fines, and an adult could check the official helpline.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel as Simran tells her?
qa.a: Jahnavi is probably alarmed but calm and proud, glad her daughter came straight to her.

grounding: A sibling watches a teen refuse a fake police call demanding secrecy and payment, tell a parent, and check through the official helpline.

The message came the week after my third job rejection, when hostel fees were due and Appa had just said, carefully, that money was tight this month.
"Hello Shankar! We loved your profile. Work-from-home data role, great salary, no interview needed. Reply YES to receive your offer letter. Only 3 seats left!" It was signed Ms Kapoor, HR, with a smiling photo and a company name that sounded real.
I read it maybe twenty times. It felt like the universe had finally noticed me. No interview. Somebody had loved my profile.
I typed YES. My thumb hovered over send.
Dilnaz, my roommate, looked over my shoulder. "Since when do companies love a profile without meeting you?" she said. "And why the rush?"
I laughed it off. But I didn't press send. Not yet.

qa.a: Only 3 seats left.

qa.a: Shankar felt rejected and anxious about fees, so the warm, easy offer felt like relief and recognition.

qa.a: Pause, look up the company's official website and number independently, and check with Dilnaz or the college placement cell.

qa.a: Dilnaz sees the warning signs, praise without a meeting and a rush, and feels uneasy for her roommate.

Hostel warden's note, 7 August
At about 4 p.m. I found Harsha in the hostel lobby on a call, pacing and pale. Sangeeta, a friend from the same floor, stood beside him looking worried. The caller claimed to be from a courier company: a parcel from abroad was held in customs under Harsha's name, and a "clearance fee" had to be paid within the hour or the police would be informed.
Harsha told me later he had been waiting for a birthday parcel from his brother in Dubai, so it sounded real.
I asked him to put the call on hold. We checked the courier company's official website together; its number was different. When we called it, they had no such parcel.
Harsha was shaken and embarrassed. I told him scammers target exactly this kind of moment and that asking for help was right. We reported the number to the cyber-crime helpline together.

qa.q: What did the caller say was held in customs?
qa.a: A parcel from abroad under Harsha's name.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling during the call?
qa.a: He felt panicked and pressured, pale and pacing, because he really was waiting for a parcel.

qa.q: What did the warden do that others could copy?
qa.a: Put the call on hold, found the official number independently, confirmed there was no parcel, and reported the caller.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta have felt standing beside Harsha?
qa.a: Sangeeta likely felt worried and unsure how to help, then relieved when the warden stepped in.

grounding: A warden notes how an urgent fake courier call reached a student at a moment of real expectation, seeming to come from a courier and customs.

Sunday night
Four months in Chennai and I still eat dinner alone most nights. Today a message came from a stranger on the photo app: "Your pictures of the beach are beautiful. You see the world like a poet." His name is Arvind; he says he's an engineer on a ship, travelling. We talked for three hours. He asked about my day, remembered the name of my cat back home, and said he had never met anyone so easy to talk to.
I felt warm all evening, as if someone had switched on a lamp in my room.
Ganga aunty, my landlady, asked why I was smiling at my phone. I didn't tell her. I don't know why. It's probably nothing. He says he'll call tomorrow from the ship.
I'm going to sleep with the phone near my pillow.
Vandana

qa.a: An engineer on a ship.

passage:
Counsellor's note, 22 November
Vidya, second-year physics, came in with her classmate Yash, who persuaded her to talk. For six weeks she has been chatting with a man online who calls himself a trading mentor. He sends her good-morning messages, remembers her exam dates, and says she has "a rare mind for markets". Early on she put a small amount into his site; it grew, and she was able to withdraw a little. That convinced her.
She said, "I'm top of my class. I'm not someone who falls for things." Yash told me she had planned to put in her whole semester allowance this week.
I told her clearly that clever, careful people are targeted precisely because these schemes work on feelings, not intelligence. She was upset and embarrassed.
Same day: we called the cyber-crime helpline together, and she agreed to phone her parents from my office this evening. I will see her again on Monday.

qa.q: How long has Vidya been chatting with the man?
qa.a: For six weeks.

qa.q: What does Vidya's line about being top of her class reveal?
qa.a: She feels proud and defensive, sure her intelligence protects her, which makes the emotional pull harder to see.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do the same day, and why?
qa.a: Called the cyber-crime helpline with Vidya and arranged a call to her parents, so she was not left alone before sending more money.

qa.q: What might Yash have felt bringing Vidya to the counsellor?
qa.a: Yash was probably worried and a bit nervous about upsetting her, but determined to protect a friend.

grounding: A counsellor notes how warmth, small proofs and flattery made a clever student trust an online scammer, since the scheme worked on emotion.
